## One group objective and observable capabilities

<p>Trace resource lifetime and use evidence to distinguish expected retention from a leak.</p>

<ul>
<li>Separate memory reclamation from explicit resource cleanup.</li>
<li>Assign owned and borrowed resource responsibilities.</li>
<li>Design a retention investigation and a check of the proposed repair.</li>
</ul>

**Prerequisites**

No catalog prerequisite. Establish the terms and scenario assumptions in the foundation questions before progressing; a published lesson is not evidence that you know them.

<p>Begin with who creates, holds and releases a resource. That ownership model supplies the hypotheses for growing memory: inspect what remains alive and why before concluding that the collector or one component is at fault.</p>

### S01-Q029 · Mechanism

<p>How would you explain the roles of the Garbage Collector, IDisposable and deterministic cleanup in a .NET component that owns resources?</p>

**Source:** [S01-Q029](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q029)

<p class="scope-note">Version-sensitive scope: state the actual runtime/framework/provider and check official documentation before making technical claims. This question bank does not certify current behavior, product defaults or performance results.</p>

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S01-Q029](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q029)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> What roles do Garbage Collector, `IDisposable`, and deterministic cleanup play?

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Separate reclaiming memory from ending a resource’s useful lifetime. Deterministic cleanup means an explicit cleanup boundary rather than relying on an unspecified later moment.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Assign ownership and cleanup responsibilities clearly.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Name managed and external resources, ownership and runtime; consult official documentation for finalization, disposal and framework-specific ownership rules.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Traces creation, use and cleanup, including an exception path.</li>
<li>Distinguishes owned and borrowed resources and explains how cleanup behavior would be checked.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Assuming garbage collection makes resource ownership or disposal unnecessary.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>Who should perform cleanup when the component receives a resource it did not create?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S01-Q028"></a>

### S01-Q028 · Failure cases

<p>A .NET application’s memory use grows over time. How would you determine whether it is a leak, expected retention or another resource issue?</p>

**Source:** [S01-Q028](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q028)

<p class="scope-note">Version-sensitive scope: state the actual runtime/framework/provider and check official documentation before making technical claims. This question bank does not certify current behavior, product defaults or performance results.</p>

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S01-Q028](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q028)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> How would you diagnose a memory leak in a .NET application?

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Start from a reproducible symptom and competing explanations. Retention means objects or resources remain reachable or held; the cause must be established with evidence.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Design a memory investigation that distinguishes causes.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>State runtime, workload and the memory metric that grows; check official tooling documentation before interpreting counters, snapshots or collection behavior.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Compares observations over time and identifies what keeps suspect state alive.</li>
<li>Explains a test that could falsify the diagnosis and verifies the change under comparable load.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Calling every increase in process memory a managed-memory leak.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>What would you check if managed-heap observations did not explain process growth?</li>
</ul>

</details>

## Combined production exercise — agent-added

<p>A hypothetical .NET service retains more memory after repeated file-processing requests. Draw resource ownership and cleanup on success and failure, identify competing managed and external-resource explanations, and propose snapshots or measurements that distinguish them. State runtime/tool assumptions and the comparable rerun needed after a repair.</p>

## Short rubric — use only with an actual attempt

**Basic answer**

<p>Explains ownership and cleanup with a coherent lifecycle.</p>

**Senior answer**

<p>Uses retention evidence and falsifiable hypotheses, then checks the repair on equivalent work.</p>

**Still needs evidence**

<p>Rising process memory or a forced collection alone does not prove the diagnosis or fix.</p>
